Handle with care: if you want to cook to customer order, pursue dish innovation, or are unwilling to handle dietary restrictions, allergens and usage records, the actual work will not match expectations.

The core output is bulk meals delivered on time, in the right portions and meeting dietary restrictions, together with verifiable usage and temperature-control records, not “being able to make a particular dish” or “being able to operate a particular machine”.

Menu and prep, bulk cooking and portioning, and cleaning and inventory are editorial work areas on this page, not three official occupations. Currently 17 tasks 12/5 Core and Supplemental: temperature monitoring and recording, cooking to the menu and dietary restrictions, storage rotation, washing utensils, portioning, cleaning checks, handling meat, fish and poultry, directing assisting staff, training new staff, taking inventory, requesting purchases and baking are Core; government food commodity procedures, menu design, menu expenditure monitoring, usage and expenditure records and meal price calculation are Supplemental. Importance is not frequency, and menu design and staff training cannot be excluded wholesale as adjacent management duties. Specific menus, special meals, records and division of labour are checked against the unit and the applicable food-safety requirements, and actual positions are not guaranteed to perform all of them.
Menu and prep

Check the menu and dietary restrictions against the meal plan → estimate portion counts from the number of diners → receive ingredients and check shelf life by batch → weigh and cut to the recipe → handle meat, fish and poultry and isolate allergen-related ingredients → label the production time and batch
Prep and portion-count records, confirmation of dietary restrictions and allergen isolation
Bulk cooking and portioning

Confirm equipment cleanliness and operating status → heat, bake and hold in bulk according to the meal service period → check core temperature and doneness → portion or pack by portion → deliver on the serving line, at the window or in the ward → record finished-product temperature and the number of portions served
Bulk output and temperature-control records, confirmation of stopping service and reporting on exceptions
Cleaning, inventory and records

Core: cleaning checks, taking inventory and submitting requests and storage rotation; Supplemental: usage and expenditure records. The handover format is checked against the institution's procedure, and face-to-face sign-off is not uniformly required.
Where is the boundary between institution and cafeteria cooks and adjacent catering positions?

This table compares institution and cafeteria cooks with adjacent catering positions item by item across seven dimensions: core purpose, main object and basis, core process, main output, responsible party, collaboration and supervision, and boundaries of conclusion; adjacent positions all work in food preparation settings, but menu decision-making, whether cooking is done to customer order, whether usage and expenditure records are kept, and the food-safety and temperature-control chain of responsibility do not transfer simply because positions are adjacent; comparisons must check the actual duties item by item.
Core purpose
Within fixed meal service periods, cook in bulk and portion meals to a menu and dietary restrictions for an institutional population, and leave verifiable usage and temperature-control records.

Adjacent chefs and managers lean towards menus, operations and staff organisation; restaurant and fast food are checked separately by order scope. Food preparation includes prep, food assembly, temperature recording and some preparation, and dishwashers also have cleaning and prep tasks, so the duties of adjacent positions cannot be called completely mutually exclusive.
Main object and basis

A cyclical menu, dietary and nutritional restrictions, the number of diners and portion counts, ingredient batches and temperature-control records; the basis is the meal plan, food-safety requirements and the institution's operating rules.

Objects and bases of adjacent positions: menus and cost sheets (chefs and managers), full recipes and orders (restaurant cooks), fast food recipes and order tickets (fast food cooks), prep lists (preparation workers), and tableware and cleaning processes (dishwashers).
Core process
Check the menu and dietary restrictions → estimate portion counts and prep → cook and hold in bulk → monitor finished-product temperature → portion and deliver → clean, take inventory and record.

Processes of adjacent positions: menu and cost accounting, scheduling and purchasing, continuous heating and plating to order, bulk heating and boxing to order, washing, cutting and preparing, and cleaning, disinfection and putting things away.
Main output
Bulk meals delivered on time, in the right portions and meeting dietary restrictions, together with verifiable usage, discard and temperature-control records.

Outputs of adjacent positions: a costable menu and gross margin, operating reports, per-customer dishes, fast food finished products, prepared semi-finished ingredients, and clean tableware and premises.
Responsible party

Menus, dietary restrictions, portion counts, temperature control and hygiene are carried out according to the actual duties; Core includes directing assisting staff and training new staff, and Supplemental includes menu design, expenditure and meal price calculation. Food production and operation operators and their principal persons in charge bear the statutory responsibility, with specific approvals and the division of staff duties checked separately, and the occupational title alone cannot exclude all management collaboration.

Each position's responsibility follows the actual division of labour and applicable regulations; food preparation and dishwashing also carry food hygiene duties; institution cooks already have coaching and some menu expenditure tasks, so not all management responsibility belongs only to adjacent occupations.
Collaboration and supervision

Collaborate by station and by the prep-to-service periods within the canteen, possibly directing colleagues who assist with prep and portioning; when temperature anomalies, foreign objects or allergen problems are found, stop the affected work and report to the supervisor.

Collaboration of adjacent positions: chefs and managers assign tasks and schedules; restaurant cooks align timing with the plating and food-running roles; fast food cooks check orders with the counter; preparation workers receive prep specification requirements.
Boundaries of conclusion

Similar position names do not mean interchangeable roles: whether the menu is designed independently, whether usage and expenditure records are kept, and whether meals are served to a fixed population determine the scope of authorisation and where responsibility lies.

The preparation levels and qualification requirements of adjacent positions do not apply to this occupation and must be checked item by item against each occupation's official material and the employer's rules.
Key occupational judgements

Six recurring professional judgements: whether the menu and dietary restrictions are checked; whether portions and portion counts match the meal plan; whether bulk heating and holding meet the standard; whether allergens and raw-cooked zoning are isolated; whether cleaning, storage and inventory rotation follow procedure; and whether usage records and exceptions are reported according to procedure and handed over to the next shift.

Before service, check the menu, allergens and dietary restrictions item by item (low salt, sugar-free, liquid, food avoidances and so on) and confirm the number of diners and portions; treating dietary restrictions as a verbal reminder rather than applying them to the meal will pass the risk on to the people who need restricted diets.

Weighing, cutting and portioning must be carried out and rechecked to the meal plan and portion standards; estimating by feel leads to too few portions or waste from cooking too much, and also makes the subsequent usage records meaningless.

Check heating and holding time and temperature by dish, equipment and applicable food-safety requirements and record them; appearance does not prove that suspect contaminated food is safe, and this round obtained no ranking of common hazards or a uniform time limit.

Ingredients, utensils and stations containing allergens must be handled and labelled separately, with raw and cooked kept apart; using a shared station without cleaning it first passes the risk on to unaware diners.
Judgement four: have allergens and the raw-cooked zones been isolated?

Equipment, tableware and work areas must be treated according to the cleaning and disinfection procedure, and ingredients must be rotated first-in-first-out with the time labelled, and those near their expiry date used first; skipping disinfection or putting new stock in first leaves the problem for the next shift.
Judgement five: do cleaning, storage and inventory rotation follow procedure?

For exceptions, stop the affected work, isolate, escalate and hand over the conditions still to be checked according to the actual procedure; Article 47 of the Food Safety Law provides that where an operator faces a potential risk of an incident it must stop operating and report to the regulatory department, and an internal report alone cannot substitute for the statutory report.

Menu and dietary restrictions ｜ check the menu against the meal plan ｜ plan portion counts according to the cyclical menu and the number of diners, check dietary and nutritional restrictions, allergens and food avoidances, and apply the restrictions to specific meals and dish positions; when the menu or the number of diners changes, confirm with the supervisor before adjusting.

Prep and weighing ｜ prepare to recipe and portion counts ｜ receive ingredients and check shelf life by batch, weigh and cut to recipe, handle meat, fish and poultry, portion by count and isolate and label allergen-related ingredients.

Bulk cooking and portioning ｜ produce in bulk within the meal service period ｜ heat, bake, steam and hold in bulk according to equipment capacity, check core temperature and doneness, portion or pack by portion, and deliver on the serving line, at the window or in the ward within the meal service period.

Temperature control and hygiene ｜ monitor temperature and maintain hygiene ｜ monitor and record refrigeration, freezer, heating and holding temperatures according to food-safety requirements, clean and inspect kitchen equipment, tableware and work areas, clean and disinfect utensils and chopping boards according to procedure, and store raw and cooked ingredients in separate zones.

Core: taking inventory, requesting ingredients and equipment, and rotating storage; Supplemental: monitoring menu expenditure, usage and expenditure records, meal price calculation and government food commodity procedures. Specific duties and record formats are checked with the institution, and Supplemental tasks are not all written as Core.

Core: directing staff who assist with prep and portioning and training new employees; Supplemental: menu design and cost-effectiveness monitoring. Management collaboration may exist but does not automatically grant all the authority of an adjacent supervisor.
Work context and working conditions
Institution and cafeteria cooks usually work standing for long periods in a climate-controlled indoor kitchen, facing heat, humidity, noise and the deadlines of fixed meal service times;

Current institution cook 57 work context questions: 90% daily in a climate-controlled indoor environment; 80% never in a non-climate-controlled indoor environment and 93% never outdoors in all weather, with incomplete daily responses for the last two questions, so 8% or 0 is not filled in. Different questions may overlap, and the actual conditions of central kitchens and canteens are checked on site and are not uniform Chinese conditions.

Main materials and equipment ｜ cyclical menus and dietary restriction lists, ingredients and seasonings, bulk cooking equipment (steamers, ovens, stockpots and frying equipment), holding and refrigeration and freezer equipment, portioning and serving line equipment, tableware and washing equipment, thermometers and cleaning and disinfection supplies; the equipment list comes from this occupation's tasks and work activities and is not a purchasing recommendation.

During the prep period, cook and hold in bulk to the menu, and during the service period portion and deliver; when temperature anomalies, foreign objects or insufficient portions occur, stop the affected work and report; after service, clean equipment, store ingredients first-in-first-out and record usage and temperature control.

Currently 79%/13%, almost constantly and more than half the time, for standing; 70% use their hands almost constantly; 36%/26%, almost constantly and more than half the time, for repetitive motion; and 83% face daily strict time limits. The equipment pace question shows 16%/16%/51%, extremely important, fairly important and not important, with other responses not shown and no total for unshown responses filled in. Work week: 16% over 40 hours / 42% about 40 hours / 41% under 40 hours; 95% have a regular schedule; not all canteens have the same rotation.

Currently teamwork 67%/17%, extremely important and very important; coordinating and leading 23%/38%, extremely important and very important; contact with others 77%/15%, continually and most of the time; and 83% take part in daily face-to-face discussions. The U.S. respondent answers to individual questions are not shares of working hours, an intersection of the same people or Chinese requirements; the actual reporting department is checked with the institution.

Currently responsibility for others' health and safety 49%/25%, very high and high, and 63% make daily decisions; consequences of error 27%/26%/11%/17%/19%, extremely serious, very serious, serious, fairly serious and not serious. This reflects the subjective work context, not an accident rate or a proportion of statutory responsibility, and documentation and escalation are checked against the institution and the law.

Currently 66% have daily routine protection, accuracy 28%/40%/28%, extremely important, very important and important, and 58% never sit. The supply question lists several categories, which does not mean everyone wears all of them; actual protection, temperature control and health conditions are checked against applicable regulations and on-site assessment.

Institution and cafeteria cooks (Cooks, Institution and Cafeteria) is the occupation that cooks and portions in bulk for fixed populations such as schools, hospitals, elder-care facilities and enterprise and institutional canteens, corresponding to U.S. O*NET-SOC 35-2012.00: the work includes cooking to the menu and dietary or nutritional restrictions, portioning or packing by portion count and portion, cleaning equipment and work areas, washing tableware, monitoring and recording food temperature, rotating and storing first-in-first-out, taking inventory and ordering and receiving as needed, and recording usage and expenditure; it may also involve scheduling colleagues who assist with prep and portioning and training new staff. The China section of this page uses verifiable entities such as the Chinese cuisine chef (occupation code 4-03-02-01) as leads: the two occupational classifications are not one-to-one, and this page does not apply U.S. preparation levels, qualifications or wages directly to mainland China, nor does it merge the duties of restaurant cooks, fast food cooks, food preparation workers or dishwashers into this occupation.
Prepare short-order dishes to customer order on the spot at a counter or short order station, while handling orders, plating and simple payment.
Mainly upstream work such as washing, cutting and preparation, usually without independent responsibility for cooking to the menu and portioning.
Wash tableware, kitchens, food preparation equipment and utensils, and help put things away and clean the premises.
Design menus and output standards, organise the kitchen division of labour, calculate costs and manage kitchen staff, and may still cook signature dishes personally.
Restaurant cooks (O*NET-SOC 35-2014.00, adjacent segment)

Serve continuously in a restaurant back-of-house according to customer orders and the menu: the dish range is wider and there are more stations, requiring both reproducing flavours to recipe and aligning timing with the plating and food-running roles at peak times.

The key difference from institution and cafeteria cooks is serving ordering customers with dishes that change by time of day; employment was 1,460,200 in 2024, and the O*NET growth category is “much faster than average (7% or higher)”.
Better suited to people willing to collaborate on service in a faster-paced, multi-dish environment and able to accept evening and weekend shifts.
Fast food cooks (O*NET-SOC 35-2011.00, adjacent segment)
Cook and box in bulk to order tickets in a fast food restaurant with a limited menu, operating large-capacity single-purpose equipment, at a fast pace and with high repetition.
The key difference is cooking to customer order, with a fixed menu and random portion counts; employment was 669,500 in 2024, and the O*NET growth category is “decline (-14%)”.
Better suited to people who can accept a high degree of repetition, work to a standard and want to start work relatively quickly.
Short order cooks (O*NET-SOC 35-2015.00, adjacent segment)
The key difference is the shortest process, with orders directly deciding the production sequence; employment was 151,100 in 2024, and the O*NET growth category is “decline (-1% or lower)”.
Better suited to people who react quickly, can handle several short tickets at once and deal with customers directly.
Food preparation workers (O*NET-SOC 35-2021.00, adjacent occupation)

The key difference is that there is no responsibility for cooking and portioning; employment was 902,700 in 2024, the O*NET growth category is “decline (-1% or lower)”, and it often serves as the entry point into the institutional kitchen system.
Better suited to people who want to start from preparation and gradually learn bulk cooking and portioning.
Dishwashers (O*NET-SOC 35-9021.00, adjacent occupation)
The key difference is that the role does not touch food cooking or portioning and is a support position; employment was 477,700 in 2024, and the O*NET growth category is “little or no change”.
Better suited to people who want to enter an institutional catering setting first and start from a support position.
Chefs and head cooks (O*NET-SOC 35-1011.00, adjacent occupation)

The key difference from this occupation is management responsibility and menu leadership: taking on menu design and cost accounting, staff scheduling and training, and setting output standards; the preparation level is Job Zone 3, and employment was 197,300 in 2024.
Better suited to people who have built up output experience, are willing to take on staff and cost management responsibility, and want to lead the menu direction.

values: Fictional work-order material (practice input)

Fictional scenario: a fictional institutional canteen must serve 420 meals at lunch that day, of which 35 are low-salt soft meals, 12 are gluten-free and 8 are nut-free allergy meals; the shift's steamer temperature log shows an abnormal rise of 25 minutes in the morning, and the shift record says only “handled”.

Material provided: the day's menu and dietary restriction list; the diner number and meal allocation table; the shift's steamer and holding cabinet temperature records; the ingredient batch and shelf-life ledger; the allergen ingredient list; a summary of the cleaning and disinfection procedure.

Material not provided: the specific cause of the temperature anomaly, whether the affected ingredients have already been used, the approval process for deciding whether to discard them, and the shift's staffing. If these conditions are needed in the exercise, state your assumptions and whom you would need to confirm them with.
Task requirements

Write a one-page shift handling and meal service plan covering menu and dietary restriction checks, the judgement and handling of the affected ingredients, bulk cooking and holding requirements, portion counts and portioning arrangements, the situations that require stopping service or reporting, and the items to hand over to the next shift.
The plan must state which data come from the exercise material and which are still assumptions, and must say whether it relies on the menu, the temperature-control records or the procedure summary.
Reference deliverable (derivable from the exercise material)

The plan should include: checks (label each of the 55 special meals as low-salt soft, gluten-free or nut-free, and check them against the meal allocation table); ingredient judgement (ingredients in the cabinet during the morning temperature anomaly must be held back from use and reported, and must not be released on the strength of a “handled” record alone); bulk cooking and temperature control (check finished-product core temperature and holding duration against the menu); portion counts and portioning (portion according to the meal allocation table, using separate utensils and stations for special meals); exception handling (stop using the affected ingredients and report before the temperature anomaly is characterised, with authorised personnel deciding whether to discard or release them); records and handover (set out the period of the temperature anomaly, the batches involved, the action taken and the items still to be confirmed).
The reference deliverable lists only the elements that should be included and does not require wording identical to the example; explaining the basis for your judgement is enough.
Boundaries and conclusions that cannot be drawn

This exercise tests only dietary restriction checking, temperature-control awareness and the ability to organise records; it does not evaluate a real institution's meal service safety and does not constitute a hiring or qualification judgement or advice on real food-safety or dietary handling.

Real institutions' diner information, health information or business data must not be used; where real food-safety and dietary judgements are involved, the rules of the unit and the competent authority must be followed.

entries.answer: Cook in bulk to the menu and dietary or nutritional restrictions, portion and deliver by portion count and portion, monitor and record food temperature, wash pots, tableware and equipment, rotate and store first-in-first-out, take inventory and request and receive ingredients as needed, and possibly schedule colleagues who assist with prep and portioning and train new staff; school, hospital, elder-care and enterprise and institutional canteens place different emphasis on these.
entries.question: What does the daily work of institution and cafeteria cooks involve?

entries.answer: Institution and cafeteria cooks serve a fixed population in bulk to a cyclical menu and dietary restrictions and often keep usage and expenditure records; restaurant cooks serve ordering customers with a wider dish range; food preparation workers mainly do upstream preparation such as washing and cutting and do not carry cooking and portioning responsibility.
entries.question: How do institution and cafeteria cooks differ from restaurant cooks and food preparation workers?

entries.answer: Menu and usage calculation, prep forecasting, inventory and expiry alerts, and meal ordering and service scheduling can be assisted by systems, and programmed equipment and temperature logging can also reduce manual steps; but applying dietary restrictions, judging portion counts and portions, bulk heat control, allergen isolation, exception handling and handover still depend on on-site staff. Technology exposure does not equal organisational adoption or the disappearance of jobs.
entries.question: How will AI affect or replace institution and cafeteria cooks?

entries.answer: What can be checked is change at the task level: three task groups — menu, usage and inventory information, bulk cooking and service pace, and temperature control and recording — can be partly taken over by tools; this page has no occupation-specific adoption rate or displacement data.
entries.question: For which tasks of institution and cafeteria cooks is there evidence of AI-driven change?

entries.answer: Applying the menu and dietary restrictions, checking portion counts and portions, bulk temperature control and recording, exception handling and handover, and the basic operation of menu, inventory and temperature-control systems.
entries.question: Faced with AI, which abilities should institution and cafeteria cooks still focus on verifying?

entries.answer: In the United States the 2025 median hourly wage is 18.01 dollars and the median annual wage is 37,450 dollars (the single-occupation measure for 35-2012.00), with percentiles of 28,480/32,440/37,450/44,800/49,670 dollars a year; no occupation-level wage figures were obtained for mainland China, and this page treats this as a gap rather than filling it in with industry averages.
entries.question: How much do institution and cafeteria cooks generally earn, and how should this be compared?

entries.answer: The U.S. preparation level is Job Zone 1–2, and respondent education requirements show 71% stating a high school diploma or equivalent is needed, 14% a postsecondary certificate and 7% a bachelor's degree, with skills coming mainly from on-the-job training; domestically institutional canteens mostly start people in portioning and prep roles, and some units require food-safety or nutrition training.
entries.question: What education do institution and cafeteria cooks need, and how should they train?

entries.answer: There is no uniform mandatory licence in the United States; domestically health management and food-safety training are common prerequisites, and the Chinese cuisine chef skill grade is usually not a threshold for frontline institutional canteen positions, with specific requirements following the target unit's and the competent authority's rules.
entries.question: Do you have to obtain a certificate to work as an institution and cafeteria cook?

entries.answer: First complete one “menu check—bulk cooking—portioning—temperature-control record” exercise using the fictional menu on this page, or do one shadowing shift at a canteen, and then check the target unit's meal service periods, dietary restrictions and hygiene requirements.
entries.question: If you have no background and want to try institution and cafeteria cooking work, what should you do first?

entries.answer: U.S. official projections show the growth rate for this occupation over 2024—2034 as “slower than average (1% to 2%)”, with about 69,700 job openings over the same period; institutional catering hours are relatively regular, but this should be checked against the target unit type and local recruitment.
entries.question: What else should be considered when choosing institution and cafeteria cooking as an occupation now?

bls_table.说明: The 10th percentile is a low-end statistical position in this measure's annual wage distribution; it is not an entry starting wage and is not converted into individual monthly income or take-home pay; O*NET national wages: Cooks, Institution and Cafeteria 35-2012.00 (2025 wage data) ｜https://www.onetonline.org/link/localwages/35-2012.00

The 25th percentile means that about a quarter of workers earn less than that value annually; it is a statistical position and does not indicate a seniority grade or job duties; O*NET national wages: Cooks, Institution and Cafeteria 35-2012.00 (2025 wage data) ｜https://www.onetonline.org/link/localwages/35-2012.00

The median marks the midpoint of this occupation's national wage distribution; it is not an average wage, an entry wage or an employer offer; O*NET national wages: Cooks, Institution and Cafeteria 35-2012.00 (2025 wage data) ｜https://www.onetonline.org/link/localwages/35-2012.00

The 75th percentile is the position of the upper quarter of the distribution and comes from the same statistical period; it cannot be used to infer years of experience or management duties; O*NET national wages: Cooks, Institution and Cafeteria 35-2012.00 (2025 wage data) ｜https://www.onetonline.org/link/localwages/35-2012.00

The 90th percentile is a high-band position, usually associated with differences in region, institution type, shift and hours, and the source does not establish a correspondence with experience; O*NET national wages: Cooks, Institution and Cafeteria 35-2012.00 (2025 wage data) ｜https://www.onetonline.org/link/localwages/35-2012.00

BLS table 1.2 institution and cafeteria cooks 35-2012: 454,000 jobs in 2025 and a projection of 466,600 in 2035, a published net increase of 12,600 and growth of 2.8%, with an average of 62,900 openings per year (including growth and replacement). OOH and O*NET round the growth rate to 3% for the same period. This is not the family's 7% growth, and openings are not a ten-year total, net increases or current hiring; the self-employment share is not provided in the table and cannot be filled in as zero.
The growth rate is a relative change over the projection period; the net change in headcount over the same period and job openings are different measures and cannot substitute for one another.
Average annual openings include growth and replacement and are not a ten-year sum, net additions, current hiring or an individual's probability of being hired.

subject.summary: Institution and cafeteria cooks (Cooks, Institution and Cafeteria) correspond in the United States to O*NET-SOC 35-2012.00: cooking and portioning in bulk to the menu and dietary restrictions for fixed populations such as schools, hospitals, elder-care facilities and enterprise and institutional canteens, possibly also handling menu and usage calculation, ordering and receiving, inventory rotation and temperature-control records, and directing colleagues who assist with prep and portioning; on the Chinese side the Chinese cuisine chef (occupation code 4-03-02-01) and similar entities are checked separately, and the two classifications do not correspond one-to-one.
